pos: n. pl. (those who hear, especially the word preached; rendering Greek akroates and akouo, participle)
etymology: From hear, Old English hīeran. The Greek akroates is a listener at a lecture — the man in the seat, who has done nothing yet.
biblical_def: “For not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified” (Rom 2:13). “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves” (Jas 1:22). Speech is to be “good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers” (Eph 4:29). Timothy is to charge them “that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers” (2Ti 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hearer as one who hears; one who attends to what is orally delivered by another; an auditor.
webster_full: HEARER, n. One who hears; one who attends to what is orally delivered by another; an auditor; one of an audience.
scriptures: Jas 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Rom 2:13
(For not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified.
Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers.
corruption_summary: Attendance is counted as discipleship, and James says the hearer only is deceiving himself.
corruption_paragraphs: James 1:22 names the most comfortable self-deception in the church: the man who hears the word every week and does not do it, and who takes the hearing for the doing. The deception is of his own self — nobody else is fooled — and James's picture is the man who looks in a glass and walks away. Romans 2:13 was written to the Jew who possessed the law and rested in it, and the sentence is the same: not the hearers of the law are just before God. Neither verse teaches justification by works; both teach that a hearing which produces no doing was not the hearing of faith. Ephesians 4:29 turns the word on the speaker: every word is to minister grace to the hearers, which is a standard for the pew as well as the pulpit.
roots_summary: Greek akroates (G202), a hearer, listener; akouo (G191), participle, those hearing.
roots_lines: Greek akroates (G202) — a hearer; Romans 2:13, James 1:22–23, 1:25.
Greek hoi akouontes (G191) — the hearers; Ephesians 4:29, 2 Timothy 2:14, Acts 10:44.
usage: “Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves” — the man in the seat.
“Not the hearers of the law are just before God” — possession is not obedience.
“That it may minister grace unto the hearers” — the standard for every word.

pos: adj. (without limit or number; rendering Hebrew en mispar, without number, and en qets, without end)
etymology: Latin infinitus, unbounded. The Hebrew has no single word for it; the Authorized Version renders two phrases, without number and without end, and gives the first to God's understanding.
biblical_def: “Great is our Lord, and of great power: his understanding is infinite” (Psa 147:5). Eliphaz to Job: “Is not thy wickedness great? and thine iniquities infinite?” (Job 22:5). Of No: “Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers” (Nah 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infinite as without limits; unbounded; boundless; not circumscribed; applied to time, space, and qualities; and, in theology, to God alone.
webster_full: INFINITE, a. Without limits; unbounded; boundless; not circumscribed; applied to time, space and qualities. God is infinite in duration, having neither beginning nor end of existence. He is also infinite in presence, or omnipresent, and his attributes are infinite.
2. That will have no end.
3. That has a beginning in space, but is infinitely extended.
scriptures: Great is our Lord, and of great power: his understanding is infinite.
Job 22:5
Is not thy wickedness great? and thine iniquities infinite?
Nah 3:9
Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers.
corruption_summary: Man's iniquities are called infinite by a comforter who was wrong about Job, and God's understanding is called infinite by a psalm that was right.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 147:5 is the only place the Authorized Version says God is infinite in so many words, and the attribute it chooses is understanding. The verse before it is the reason: He telleth the number of the stars; He calleth them all by their names. A God whose understanding is without number has no unknown case and no surprised moment, which is the ground of providence and the death of anxiety in the same sentence. Eliphaz used the word of Job's iniquities and was wrong about the man, but the doctrine he stumbled on is true of every man: sin against an infinite God has an infinite demerit, which is why the Reformed have held that a finite punishment could not answer it and only an infinite Person could bear it. Nahum's Egypt had strength that was infinite — and was carried away captive, because there is only one infinity that keeps.
roots_summary: Hebrew en mispar (H369, H4557), there is no number; en qets (H369, H7093), there is no end.
roots_lines: Hebrew en mispar (H369 with H4557) — without number, infinite; Psalm 147:5, Nahum 3:9.
Hebrew en qets (H369 with H7093) — without end, infinite; Job 22:5.
usage: “His understanding is infinite” — no unknown case, no surprised moment.
“Thine iniquities infinite?” — wrong about Job, right about the demerit of sin.
“Her strength, and it was infinite” — and carried away captive.

pos: n. (the fold of a garment; the front of the body when seated; rendering Hebrew cheq, chotsen, and beged)
etymology: Old English læppa, a fold or flap of a garment. The lot of Proverbs 16 is thrown into the fold of the robe and taken out by the hand, and the hand is God's.
biblical_def: “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33). Nehemiah before the nobles: “Also I shook my lap, and said, So God shake out every man from his house, and from his labour, that performeth not this promise” (Neh 5:13). The son of the prophets gathered wild gourds “his lap full” and shred them into the pot (2Ki 4:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lap as the loose part of a coat; the part of clothes that plays loosely; the part of the body of a person sitting, covered by the clothes.
webster_full: LAP, n. The loose part of a coat; the lower part of a garment that plays loosely.
2. The part of clothes that lies on the knees when a person sits down; hence, the knees in this position.
scriptures: The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
Neh 5:13

Also I shook my lap, and said, So God shake out every man from his house, and from his labour, that performeth not this promise, even thus be he shaken out, and emptied. And all the congregation said, Amen, and praised the LORD. And the people did according to this promise.
And one went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine, and gathered thereof wild gourds his lap full, and came and shred them into the pot of pottage: for they knew them not.
corruption_summary: Chance is believed in, and Proverbs 16:33 says that even the lot in the lap is disposed by the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 16:33 is the shortest statement of providence in the Bible and it reaches the smallest event. The lot is cast into the lap — the nearest thing the ancient world had to pure chance, the dice in the fold of the robe — and the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD. Not the outcome of battles and the rise of kings only, which most religions grant, but the fall of the lot; there is no event too small for the decree and no randomness that is random to Him. The verse is the doctrine under Jonah's lot, Matthias's lot, and the soldiers' lot for the coat. Nehemiah's lap is the same fold used as a sign: shaken out empty, so God shake out every man that keeps not this promise — a governor's oath made with his own garment.
roots_summary: Hebrew cheq (H2436), the bosom, the lap; chotsen (H2684), the bosom of a garment; beged (H899), a garment.
roots_lines: Hebrew cheq (H2436) — bosom, lap; Proverbs 16:33.
Hebrew chotsen (H2684) — bosom, lap; Nehemiah 5:13; beged (H899), garment, lap; 2 Kings 4:39.
usage: “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” — no event too small for the decree.
“I shook my lap” — Nehemiah's oath with his own garment.
“His lap full” — wild gourds, and death in the pot.

pos: n. (the whole duration of a life; rendering Hebrew chayyim, Greek zoe and zao)
etymology: Life + time. The Authorized Version uses it three times, and two of them are about what a lifetime can be wasted on.
biblical_def: Abraham to the rich man: “Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented” (Luk 16:25). Christ took flesh to “deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” (Heb 2:15). “Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself a pillar, which is in the king's dale: for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance” (2Sa 18:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lifetime as the time that life continues; duration of life.
webster_full: LIFETIME, n. The time that life continues; duration of life.
scriptures: But Abraham said, Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.
Heb 2:15
And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.

Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself a pillar, which is in the king's dale: for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance: and he called the pillar after his own name: and it is called unto this day, Absalom's place.
corruption_summary: A lifetime of good things is taken as God's favour, and Abraham told the rich man it was the whole of what he would get.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 16:25 is the sentence on a prosperous lifetime. The rich man had received his good things, and the word is received — as a payment, in full, in the only place he would get them — and Lazarus had received his evil things, and now the accounts were reversed and fixed. The verse does not say the rich man was damned for being rich; it says his lifetime was the whole of his portion, because he had chosen it so. Hebrews 2:15 describes the lifetime of everyone else before Christ: subject to bondage through fear of death, all their lifetime, a slavery that begins at the first funeral and does not end until the resurrection is believed. Absalom's lifetime was spent rearing a pillar to keep his name, and his name is kept — by the pillar's story, in a dale, with his hair in an oak.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayyim (H2416), life, lifetime; Greek zoe (G2222), life; zao (G2198), to live.
roots_lines: Greek en te zoe sou (G2222) — in thy lifetime; Luke 16:25; dia pantos tou zen (G2198), through all their lifetime; Hebrews 2:15.
Hebrew bechayyav (H2416) — in his lifetime; 2 Samuel 18:18.
usage: “Thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things” — received, in full, in the only place he would get them.
“All their lifetime subject to bondage” — the slavery that begins at the first funeral.
“Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself a pillar” — and his name is kept.

etymology: Latin miserabilis, to be pitied. Paul's Greek is the same: if there is no resurrection, Christians are of all men most to be pitied.
biblical_def: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable” (1Co 15:19). To Laodicea: “thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked” (Rev 3:17). Job to his three friends: “I have heard many such things: miserable comforters are ye all” (Job 16:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines miserable as very unhappy from grief, pain, calamity, poverty, or apprehension of evil; wretched; very poor, worthless.
webster_full: MISERABLE, a. Very unhappy from grief, pain, calamity, poverty, apprehension of evil, or other cause. It however expresses somewhat less than wretched.
2. Very poor; worthless.
3. Causing unhappiness or misery.
scriptures: If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.
Rev 3:17
Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:
Job 16:2
I have heard many such things: miserable comforters are ye all.
corruption_summary: Christianity is recommended as a better life now, and Paul said that if that were all, Christians would be of all men most miserable.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 15:19 destroys the gospel of the better life. If in this life only we have hope in Christ — if the resurrection is not true and the faith is a way of living well between two darknesses — then Christians are the most pitiable men alive, because they have given up the world for a lie. Paul does not say Christianity would still be worthwhile; he says it would be a disaster. Every apologetic that sells the faith on its earthly benefits has accepted the condition Paul refused. Revelation 3:17 is the other miserable, the one that does not know it: Laodicea rich and increased with goods, and wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked in the sight of the One who counts. Job's friends are the third use, and the church still produces them — miserable comforters, whose theology was orthodox and whose application was cruelty.
roots_summary: Greek eleeinos (G1652), pitiable, to be pitied; Hebrew amal (H5999), toil, trouble, misery.
roots_lines: Greek eleeinos (G1652) — pitiable, miserable; 1 Corinthians 15:19, Revelation 3:17 only.
Hebrew amal (H5999) — trouble, misery; Job 16:2, “comforters of trouble.”
usage: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable” — the gospel of the better life refused.
“Thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked” — Laodicea's true inventory.
“Miserable comforters are ye all” — orthodox, and cruel.

pos: n. (a compound of substances; of wine, spiced; rendering Hebrew mesek, Greek migma and akratos)
etymology: Latin mixtura. The cup of Psalm 75 is full of mixture, spiced to strength; the cup of Revelation 14 is poured out without mixture, wrath undiluted.
biblical_def: “For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them” (Psa 75:8). The worshipper of the beast “shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation” (Rev 14:10). Nicodemus “brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight” (John 19:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mixture as the act of mixing; a mass or compound formed by different substances put together; an ingredient added and mixed.
webster_full: MIXTURE, n. The act of mixing, or state of being mixed.
2. A mass or compound, consisting of different ingredients blended without order.
3. An ingredient added and mixed.
scriptures: The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb:
Psa 75:8

For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them.
John 19:39
And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight.
corruption_summary: Hell is imagined as wrath diluted by mercy, and Revelation 14:10 pours the cup out without mixture.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 14:10 answers the hope that the wrath to come will be tempered. The wine of the wrath of God is poured out without mixture — the Greek is unmixed, the strong wine the ancients always cut with water, served here neat — into the cup of His indignation. In this life every judgment is mixed with mercy; the rain falls on the unjust and the sun rises on the evil, and men mistake the dilution for the drink. The cup of Psalm 75 is the same cup in this age, full of mixture, spiced, poured out a little at a time, and the dregs kept for the wicked to wring out at the end. Nicodemus's mixture is the word's gentlest use: a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes for the body of the One who drank the cup without mixture for His people, so that they would never taste it.
roots_summary: Hebrew mesek (H4538), a mixture, spiced wine; Greek akratos (G194), unmixed, without mixture; migma (G3395), a mixture.
roots_lines: Hebrew mesek (H4538) — mixture, spiced wine; Psalm 75:8.
Greek akratos (G194) — unmixed; Revelation 14:10 only; migma (G3395), John 19:39.
usage: “Poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation” — wrath served neat.
“The wine is red; it is full of mixture” — the cup of this age, and the dregs kept.
“A mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight” — for the body of the One who drank the other cup.

pos: v. (leaned upon, trusted in; rendering Hebrew sha'an, to lean)
etymology: Latin religare, to bind fast, through French. The Hebrew is the same verb as lean in Proverbs 3:5, and Asa's life is its commentary.
biblical_def: Of Abijah's victory: “the children of Judah prevailed, because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers” (2Ch 13:18). Hanani the seer to Asa: “Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand” (2Ch 16:7); “Were not the Ethiopians and the Lubims a huge host…? yet, because thou didst rely on the LORD, he delivered them into thine hand” (2Ch 16:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rely as to rest on something, as the mind when satisfied of the veracity, integrity, or ability of persons; to depend; to trust; to have confidence in.
webster_full: RELY, v.i. To rest on something, as the mind when satisfied of the veracity, integrity or ability of persons, or of the certainty of facts or of evidence; to have confidence; to trust; to depend.
scriptures: And at that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah, and said unto him, Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand.
Were not the Ethiopians and the Lubims a huge host, with very many chariots and horsemen? yet, because thou didst rely on the LORD, he delivered them into thine hand.
Thus the children of Israel were brought under at that time, and the children of Judah prevailed, because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers.
corruption_summary: A man who relied on the LORD against a million Ethiopians relied on Syria against Baasha, and the seer told him the second was the greater danger.
corruption_paragraphs: Asa is the Bible's study in reliance, and the lesson is that it does not carry over. In his youth he relied on the LORD against a huge host and was delivered; in his old age, against a smaller enemy, he sent the temple silver to Syria and relied on Benhadad, and the seer's rebuke in 2 Chronicles 16 is one of the most searching in the Old Testament: the eyes of the LORD run to and fro through the whole earth to shew Himself strong on behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward Him — herein thou hast done foolishly. Asa put the seer in prison, and the chapter ends with the king diseased in his feet and seeking not the LORD but the physicians. Reliance is a present tense; yesterday's is no credit today, and a smaller crisis is where a man who once relied on God finds out whether he still does.
roots_summary: Hebrew sha'an (H8172), to lean, support oneself, rely.
roots_lines: Hebrew sha'an, niphal (H8172) — to lean upon, rely; 2 Chronicles 13:18, 16:7–8, Proverbs 3:5, Isaiah 10:20, 50:10.
usage: “Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God” — the seer to Asa.
“Because thou didst rely on the LORD, he delivered them into thine hand” — the same man, years before.
“Prevailed, because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers” — Judah under Abijah.

pos: n. (the corrosion of metal; rendering Greek brosis, eating, and ios, rust, poison)
etymology: Old English rūst. The Lord's Greek in Matthew 6 is eating — the moth and the eating that corrupt — and James's is the rust that testifies.
biblical_def: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:19–20). James to the rich: “Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as it were fire. Ye have heaped treasure together for the last days” (Jas 5:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rust as the oxyd of a metal; a substance composed of oxygen combined with a metal, and forming a rough coat on its surface; loss of power by inactivity; foul matter contracted.
webster_full: RUST, n. The oxyd of a metal; a substance composed of oxygen combined with a metal, and forming a rough coat on its surface.
2. Loss of power by inactivity, as metals lose their brightness and smoothness when not used.
3. Any foul matter contracted; as rust on corn or salted meat.
scriptures: Mat 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
Jas 5:3
Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as it were fire. Ye have heaped treasure together for the last days.
corruption_summary: Wealth is stored as security, and the Lord said the storehouse has two tenants, moth and rust, and James said the rust would testify.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 6:19 is not against having but against laying up, and its argument is a survey of the storehouse: moth in the cloth, rust in the metal, thieves at the wall. Every earthly treasure has a natural enemy already inside it, and the man who trusts the pile has trusted something that is being eaten while he sleeps. The Lord's alternative is not poverty but a different vault, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and the sentence that follows is the diagnosis: where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. James 5:3 makes the rust a witness. Gold does not rust, and James says theirs has — the hoard kept back from the labourers has corroded in the keeping, and the corrosion will testify at the last day and eat the flesh of the hoarder like fire. Treasure heaped for the last days is treasure heaped against them.
roots_summary: Greek brosis (G1035), eating, corrosion, rust; ios (G2447), rust, poison.
roots_lines: Greek brosis (G1035) — eating, rust; Matthew 6:19–20.
Greek ios (G2447) — rust, poison; James 5:3; and poison, Romans 3:13, James 3:8.
usage: “Where moth and rust doth corrupt” — the enemy already inside the storehouse.
“The rust of them shall be a witness against you” — gold that corroded in the keeping.
“Ye have heaped treasure together for the last days” — and against them.

pos: v. (to slip, to lose footing; rendering Hebrew mot and ma'ad)
etymology: Old English slīdan. Deuteronomy 32:35 — their foot shall slide in due time — is the text of the most famous sermon ever preached in America.
biblical_def: The song of Moses: “To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste” (Deu 32:35). Of the righteous: “The law of his God is in his heart; none of his steps shall slide” (Psa 37:31). David: “I have trusted also in the LORD; therefore I shall not slide” (Psa 26:1). Hosea: “Israel slideth back as a backsliding heifer” (Hos 4:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines slide as to move along the surface of any body by slipping; to slip, to pass unobserved; to pass silently and gradually from one state to another.
webster_full: SLIDE, v.i. To move along the surface of any body by slipping, or without walking or rolling; to slip; to glide.
2. To move along the surface without stepping.
3. To pass inadvertently.
4. To pass silently and gradually from one state to another, usually from a better to a worse.
scriptures: To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence; their foot shall slide in due time: for the day of their calamity is at hand, and the things that shall come upon them make haste.
The law of his God is in his heart; none of his steps shall slide.
Psa 26:1
A Psalm of David. Judge me, O LORD; for I have walked in mine integrity: I have trusted also in the LORD; therefore I shall not slide.
Hos 4:16
For Israel slideth back as a backsliding heifer: now the LORD will feed them as a lamb in a large place.
corruption_summary: The wicked stand and take their standing for safety, and Moses says the foot shall slide in due time.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 32:35 is the verse under Jonathan Edwards's sermon, and the sermon was only the verse explained. The wicked are standing; nothing holds them up but the ground under their feet; and the ground is a slope, and the sliding is appointed — in due time — so that the only reason they have not yet fallen is that the time has not yet come. Their standing is not their safety but God's delay. Psalm 37:31 gives the other foot, and what keeps it: the law of his God is in his heart; none of his steps shall slide. The righteous man's steps hold because of what is in him, not because the slope is gentler; Hosea's heifer slides back because she has nothing in her but her own will, and a backsliding heifer is the prophet's exact word for a nation that had once been led.
roots_summary: Hebrew mot (H4131), to totter, slip, slide; ma'ad (H4571), to waver, slip; sarar (H5637), to be stubborn, slide back.
roots_lines: Hebrew mot (H4131) — to slide, be moved; Deuteronomy 32:35, Psalm 26:1.
Hebrew ma'ad (H4571) — to slip, slide; Psalm 37:31; sarar (H5637), to backslide; Hosea 4:16.
usage: “Their foot shall slide in due time” — standing is not safety but delay.
“The law of his God is in his heart; none of his steps shall slide” — what holds the other foot.
“Israel slideth back as a backsliding heifer” — a nation that had once been led.

pos: adj. (giving no firm footing; rendering Hebrew chalaqlaqqoth, smooth, slippery places)
etymology: From slip. The Hebrew is a doubled form of smooth — the places God set the wicked in were smooth as flattery, and they went down.
biblical_def: Asaph, after the sanctuary: “Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction. How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment!” (Psa 73:18–19). David of his enemies: “Let their way be dark and slippery: and let the angel of the LORD persecute them” (Psa 35:6). Of the prophets of Jerusalem: “their way shall be unto them as slippery ways in the darkness: they shall be driven on, and fall therein” (Jer 23:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines slippery as smooth, glib, so smooth as to cause slipping; not affording firm footing or confidence; not to be depended on; uncertain.
webster_full: SLIPPERY, a. Smooth; glib; having the quality opposite to roughness; as a slippery stone.
2. So smooth as to cause slipping or slipping on it; as a slippery road.
3. Not affording firm footing or confidence; that cannot be depended on; uncertain.
scriptures: Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction.
Psa 35:6
Let their way be dark and slippery: and let the angel of the LORD persecute them.
Wherefore their way shall be unto them as slippery ways in the darkness: they shall be driven on, and fall therein: for I will bring evil upon them, even the year of their visitation, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: The prosperity of the wicked is envied as high ground, and Asaph saw from the sanctuary that it was a slope.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 73 is the believer's envy cured. Asaph had watched the wicked prosper — no bands in their death, eyes standing out with fatness, more than heart could wish — and his feet had almost gone, until he went into the sanctuary of God and understood their end. The understanding is verse 18: Thou didst set them in slippery places. The high ground he had envied was a smooth slope with nothing to hold, and the height was the drop. The doctrine is that the prosperity of the wicked is not a failure of providence but a form of it; God sets them there, and the setting is the sentence. Jeremiah 23:12 gives the same slope to the prophets who preached peace: slippery ways in the darkness, driven on, and falling. Dark and slippery is the way of every man whose footing is what he owns.
roots_summary: Hebrew chalaqlaqqoth (H2519), smooth, slippery places, from chalaq, smooth, flattering.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalaqlaqqoth (H2519) — slippery places; Psalm 35:6, 73:18, Jeremiah 23:12, Daniel 11:21 (flatteries), 11:34.
usage: “Surely thou didst set them in slippery places” — the high ground was a slope.
“Let their way be dark and slippery” — David's prayer against his pursuers.
“Slippery ways in the darkness: they shall be driven on, and fall” — the prophets of peace.

pos: adv. (in the AV, formerly, once, at one time; rendering Greek pote)
etymology: Some + times. In 1611 the word meant at a former time, and Paul's three uses are all about what believers once were.
biblical_def: “But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ” (Eph 2:13). “For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light” (Eph 5:8). “For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another” (Tit 3:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sometimes as at times, at intervals, now and then; and, in an older sense, at one time, formerly.
webster_full: SOMETIMES, adv. At times; at intervals; not always; now and then.
2. At one time; opposed to another time.
3. Formerly; once; as, ye who sometimes were far off.
scriptures: Eph 2:13
But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.
Eph 5:8
For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light:
Tit 3:3
For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
corruption_summary: The modern reader hears occasionally and the AV means formerly, and the difference is the whole doctrine of conversion.
corruption_paragraphs: Read with the modern ear, Ephesians 5:8 says that Christians are darkness now and then; read with the translators' ear it says they were darkness — once, formerly, in a state that is over — and are now light in the Lord. The word marks a boundary, and every use of it in Paul stands at the line between what a man was and what grace made him: sometimes far off, now made nigh; sometimes darkness, now light; sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived — and then, in Titus 3:4, but after that the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared. Conversion in the New Testament is a past tense with a wall behind it, and the Authorized Version's sometimes is the wall. A Christianity that reads the word as occasionally has lost the wall and kept the darkness.
roots_summary: Greek pote (G4218), once, formerly, at one time.
roots_lines: Greek pote (G4218) — formerly, sometimes; Ephesians 2:13, 5:8, Titus 3:3, Colossians 3:7 (sometime), 1 Peter 3:20.
usage: “Ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh” — formerly, with a wall behind it.
“Ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord” — not occasionally.
“We ourselves also were sometimes foolish” — and then the kindness of God appeared.

pos: n. and adj. (a small ringing sound; rendering Hebrew akas, to shake the ankle-bells, and Greek alalazo, to clang)
etymology: Imitative, of a small bell. Isaiah's daughters of Zion tinkled with their feet; Paul's loveless tongue tinkled like a cymbal.
biblical_def: “Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal” (1Co 13:1). Isaiah of the daughters of Zion: “walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet” (Isa 3:16), and “In that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet” (Isa 3:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tinkling as making a small sharp sound; and, as a noun, a small quick sharp sound.
webster_full: TINKLING, ppr. Making a small quick sharp sound.
TINKLING, n. A small quick sharp sound.
scriptures: Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
Isa 3:16
Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:
Isa 3:18
In that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon,
corruption_summary: Eloquence is prized as the mark of a gifted ministry, and Paul said that without charity it is a cymbal.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 13:1 was written to the most gifted church in the New Testament, and it puts the greatest gift at the bottom of the scale if one thing is missing. Tongues of men and of angels, without charity, are sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal — noise, and the noise of pagan worship at that, since the clanging cymbal was the instrument of the Corinthian cults. The preacher whose eloquence is admired and whose love is absent has been assessed by the apostle: he is an instrument that makes a sound. Isaiah's tinkling is the same emptiness in another form, the ornaments on the feet of the daughters of Zion, haughty, wanton-eyed, mincing as they go — and in that day the Lord took the tinkling away and gave them baldness. Both tinklings are decoration in place of substance, and both are removed.
roots_summary: Greek alalazo (G214), to clang, wail; Hebrew akas (H5913), to shake the ankle-ornaments, tinkle; akes (H5914), an anklet.
roots_lines: Greek kumbalon alalazon (G2950, G214) — a clanging cymbal; 1 Corinthians 13:1.
Hebrew akas (H5913) — to tinkle with the feet; Isaiah 3:16; akes (H5914), tinkling ornaments; Isaiah 3:18.
usage: “I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal” — the gift without the love, assessed.
“Making a tinkling with their feet” — the daughters of Zion.
“The Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments” — decoration removed.

pos: n. (an inscription; a name of honour; rendering Greek titlos, Hebrew tsiyyun)
etymology: Latin titulus, an inscription, a placard. Pilate's Greek is the Latin word itself, and the title he wrote is the one true thing the trial produced.
biblical_def: “And Pilate wrote a title, and put it on the cross. And the writing was, JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS” (John 19:19). “This title then read many of the Jews: for the place where Jesus was crucified was nigh to the city: and it was written in Hebrew, and Greek, and Latin” (John 19:20). Josiah at Bethel: “What title is that that I see? And the men of the city told him, It is the sepulchre of the man of God, which came from Judah, and proclaimed these things that thou hast done” (2Ki 23:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines title as an inscription put over any thing as a name by which it is known; the inscription in the beginning of a book; an appellation of dignity or distinction; a name of honour.
webster_full: TITLE, n. An inscription put over any thing as a name by which it is known.
2. The inscription in the beginning of a book, containing the subject of the work, and sometimes the author's name.
3. An appellation of dignity, distinction or pre-eminence given to persons; as, duke, marquis, and the like.
4. A name; an appellation.
scriptures: John 19:19
And Pilate wrote a title, and put it on the cross. And the writing was, JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS.
John 19:20
This title then read many of the Jews: for the place where Jesus was crucified was nigh to the city: and it was written in Hebrew, and Greek, and Latin.

Then he said, What title is that that I see? And the men of the city told him, It is the sepulchre of the man of God, which came from Judah, and proclaimed these things that thou hast done against the altar of Bethel.
corruption_summary: The chief priests asked Pilate to change the title to a claim, and he left it a fact, in three languages, over the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: The title on the cross was the only document of the trial that told the truth, and it was written by a pagan governor to annoy the priests. JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS — in Hebrew for the people, Greek for the world, Latin for the empire — and when the chief priests asked him to amend it to he said, I am King of the Jews, Pilate answered with the sentence John records for the ages: What I have written I have written. God used a governor's spite to proclaim His Son's kingship over the place of His death, in every language of the world that would crucify Him, and the priests could not get it taken down. Josiah's title is a smaller providence: a tomb inscription at Bethel, three hundred years old, marking the man of God who had prophesied by name the king now reading it.
roots_summary: Greek titlos (G5102), a title, inscription, from the Latin; Hebrew tsiyyun (H6725), a sign, monument, title.
roots_lines: Greek titlos (G5102) — title, inscription; John 19:19–20 only.
Hebrew tsiyyun (H6725) — a signpost, monument, title; 2 Kings 23:17, Jeremiah 31:21, Ezekiel 39:15.
usage: “Pilate wrote a title, and put it on the cross” — the one true document of the trial.
“Written in Hebrew, and Greek, and Latin” — every language of the world that crucified Him.
“What title is that that I see?” — Josiah at the prophet's tomb.

pos: v. (to discolour, defile, bring into contempt; rendering Hebrew ga'al, ga'al in the piel, and chalal)
etymology: Old French desteindre, to take out the colour; the English kept the opposite sense, to put a colour in. Isaiah 63:3 is a garment stained red.
biblical_def: The One from Edom: “I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment” (Isa 63:3). Of Tyre: “The LORD of hosts hath purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, and to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth” (Isa 23:9). Job on the day of his birth: “Let darkness and the shadow of death stain it; let a cloud dwell upon it” (Job 3:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stain as to discolor by the application of foreign matter; to spot; to tarnish; to impress with figures in colours; to blot, to soil, to disgrace.
webster_full: STAIN, v.t. To discolor by the application of foreign matter; to make foul; to spot; as, to stain the hand with dye.
2. To dye; to tinge with a different color.
3. To impress with figures, in colors different from the ground.
4. To blot; to soil; to spot with guilt or infamy; to tarnish; to bring reproach on.
scriptures: Isa 63:3

I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.
Isa 23:9
The LORD of hosts hath purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, and to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth.
Job 3:5
Let darkness and the shadow of death stain it; let a cloud dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it.
corruption_summary: The stained garments of Isaiah 63 are taken for the blood of Christ's passion, and the text says the blood is His enemies'.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 63:1–6 is often preached as the crucifixion — the red garments, the blood-sprinkled raiment — and the passage says whose blood it is. I will tread them in mine anger, and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments: the stain is the enemies', the winepress is judgment, and the day of vengeance is in His heart. The Lamb's own blood is the subject of chapter 53; chapter 63 is the same Person on the other side of the winepress, and Revelation 19:13 gives Him the same vesture dipped in blood as He comes to smite the nations. Isaiah 23:9 is the word's other object, the pride of all glory stained by a purpose of God, so that the honourable of the earth are brought into contempt — Tyre, the merchant city, with its crowning merchants, wiped like a dish. Both stains are His doing and neither is regretted.
roots_summary: Hebrew ga'al, hiphil (H1351), to defile, stain; chalal (H2490), to profane, stain the pride; Job's ga'al (H1350) in a form some read as to redeem, claim.
roots_lines: Hebrew ga'al, hiphil (H1351) — to stain, defile; Isaiah 63:3; the same root, Job 3:5, “let darkness and the shadow of death stain it.”
Hebrew chalal, piel (H2490) — to profane, stain; Isaiah 23:9.
usage: “Their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment” — the enemies' blood, not the Lamb's.
“To stain the pride of all glory” — Tyre wiped like a dish.
“Let darkness and the shadow of death stain it” — Job's curse on his birthday.

pos: v. (to twist forcibly; to press out by twisting; rendering Hebrew malaq, matsah, and zur)
etymology: Old English wringan, to twist. The priest wrung off the head of the bird; the wicked shall wring out the dregs of the cup.
biblical_def: Of the burnt offering of fowls: “the priest shall bring it unto the altar, and wring off his head, and burn it on the altar” (Lev 1:15); of the sin offering, “wring off his head from his neck, but shall not divide it asunder” (Lev 5:8). Of the cup: “the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them” (Psa 75:8). Gideon “wringed the dew out of the fleece, a bowl full of water” (Jdg 6:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wring as to twist and compress; to turn and strain with violence; to squeeze, to press; to extort; to distress, to torture.
webster_full: WRING, v.t. To twist and compress; to turn and strain with violence; as, to wring clothes in washing.
2. To squeeze; to press; to force by twisting.
3. To distress; to press with pain; to torture.
4. To extort; to force by violence.
scriptures: Psa 75:8

For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them.
Lev 1:15
And the priest shall bring it unto the altar, and wring off his head, and burn it on the altar; and the blood thereof shall be wrung out at the side of the altar:
Lev 5:8
And he shall bring them unto the priest, who shall offer that which is for the sin offering first, and wring off his head from his neck, but shall not divide it asunder:
Jdg 6:38
And it was so: for he rose up early on the morrow, and thrust the fleece together, and wringed the dew out of the fleece, a bowl full of water.
corruption_summary: The wicked are pictured refusing the cup, and Psalm 75 has them wringing out the dregs themselves.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 75:8 is a picture of judgment with the judged doing the work. The cup is in the LORD's hand, the wine is red and mixed, He pours it out — and the dregs, the thick sediment at the bottom, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out and drink. Not have them poured down their throats; wring them, with both hands, to the last drop. The verse says that the damned in the end will take their own portion, that judgment is a cup a man twists dry himself, and that the sentence is finally consented to by the one under it. The priest's wringing is the other end of the same word: the poor man's dove, its head wrung off at the altar, the smallest sacrifice the Law allowed, accepted for sin — a bird's neck instead of a man's.
roots_summary: Hebrew malaq (H4454), to wring off, nip; matsah (H4680), to wring out, drain; zur (H2115), to press, wring out.
roots_lines: Hebrew malaq (H4454) — to wring off the head; Leviticus 1:15, 5:8 only.
Hebrew matsah (H4680) — to wring out, drain; Psalm 75:8, Isaiah 51:17; zur (H2115), Judges 6:38.
usage: “All the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them” — the cup twisted dry by the one under it.
“Wring off his head, and burn it on the altar” — the poor man's dove.
“Wringed the dew out of the fleece” — Gideon's bowl.
